spus.text: Assume without loss of generality that a >= b >= c.
spus.notes: This WLOG ordering must be discharged at the end by applying all permutations.

spus.text: Then ab-c, ca-b, and bc-a are powers of 2.
The smaller ones divide the larger ones; in particular, ca-b divides ab-c.
depends_on: external: if two positive powers of 2 are ordered, the smaller divides the larger
spus.notes: The comparison ca-b <= ab-c is recoverable from a >= b >= c by one-line algebra: (ab-c)-(ca-b)=(a+1)(b-c) >= 0.

spus.text: Hence ca-b = gcd(ab-c, ca-b).
depends_on: external: if y divides x and y > 0, then gcd(x,y)=y

spus.text: gcd(ab-c, ca-b) <= gcd(ab-c, a(ca-b)+ab-c).
depends_on: external: common divisors are preserved under integer linear combinations

spus.text: gcd(ab-c, a(ca-b)+ab-c) = gcd(ab-c, c(a^2-1)).
spus.notes: This follows by expanding a(ca-b)+ab-c = a^2c-c = c(a^2-1).

spus.text: Since a^2-1 is odd, this gcd is at most c.
spus.notes: The claim a^2-1 is odd requires a even. No parity case assumption or earlier SPU establishes this.

spus.text: Therefore ca-b <= c.
But a >= b >= c, so this forces a=b=c=2.
Thus the only ordered solution is (2,2,2).

spus.text: Then ab-c >= ca-b >= bc-a.
Since all three are powers of 2, bc-a divides ca-b and ca-b divides ab-c.
First suppose a is even.
The gcd estimate gives ca-b <= c.
This gives a=b=c=2.
Now suppose all of a,b,c are odd.
The usual 2-adic estimate gives ca-b <= 2^{nu_2(a^2-1)} <= 2a+2.
Since ca-b >= 3a-b, we must have c=3.
Then a=b+2, and from ca-b >= 2(bc-a) we get a=7,b=5.
This gives (a,b,c)=(7,5,3).
Therefore the ordered solutions are (2,2,2) and (7,5,3).
